lessons.title: Preconception folic acid
lessons.objective: Prescribe preconception folic acid with the right dose, start and duration, recognise who needs a high-dose plan and separate NTD prevention from fertility promises.
lessons.closing: Folic acid prevents NTDs: standard dose for almost everyone, an individual plan for high risk, and no “extra” dose for fertility or recurrent miscarriage.

lessons.title: MTHFR and methylfolate: what the sources say
lessons.objective: Explain why a common MTHFR variant does not contraindicate folic acid and why routine genotyping or homocysteine testing is not recommended.
lessons.closing: The common variant does not change the recommendation: standard folic acid, no extra tests, and a reassuring explanation.

lessons.title: Iodine before and during pregnancy
lessons.objective: Apply the iodine recommendation in preconception, pregnancy and lactation, know that thyroid treatment does not exclude it, and avoid excess.
lessons.closing: Iodine with a window: 250 µg/day in total, a 150 µg supplement if there is a risk of deficiency, the same approach on levothyroxine or antithyroid drugs, and no sustained supplement use above 500 µg/day.

lessons.title: Vitamin D: pregnancy, fertility and losses
lessons.objective: Distinguish empiric supplementation in pregnancy, correction of a deficiency with an indication and fertility claims, separating association from efficacy and clinical pregnancy from live birth.
lessons.closing: Vitamin D: reasonable in pregnancy with low certainty, without routine screening, and without trial evidence that it improves IVF outcomes or recurrent loss.

items.title: Preconception folic acid: who, how much and when
items.core: USPSTF recommends (grade A) that everyone who plans to or could become pregnant take a daily supplement containing 0.4–0.8 mg (400–800 µg) of folic acid, from at least 1 month before conception through the first 2–3 months of pregnancy. [[ref:uspstf-2023-folic-acid]]
items.body:
Indication: prevention of neural tube defects (NTDs), not fertility enhancement. USPSTF judges with high certainty that the net benefit is substantial and that, at usual doses, folic acid is not associated with serious harms. It insists on the supplement even where foods are fortified, because dietary intake is often insufficient. [[ref:uspstf-2023-folic-acid]]

NICE agrees in substance with a slightly different schedule: 400 micrograms a day, ideally from 3 months before trying to conceive (or as soon as pregnancy is known) and for at least the first 12 weeks, even with fortified flour. [[ref:nice-2025-ng247]]
items.recall: What dose, from when and until when does USPSTF recommend folic acid?

rows.text: Plans to or could become pregnant

visual.alt: Diagram: for anyone planning or able to become pregnant, daily folic acid 400–800 µg per USPSTF or 400 µg per NICE, from at least 1 month before (ideally 3 months per NICE) until the first 2–3 months or 12 weeks of pregnancy.

items.application: Ask about folic acid at any visit with a woman who could become pregnant, not only when she says she is trying: many pregnancies are unplanned.
items.pearl: Preconception folic acid = NTD prevention. If someone sells it as “to get pregnant”, the outcome is the wrong one.

items.title: High NTD risk: an individual plan, not the standard dose
items.core: The USPSTF recommendation does not apply to people with a previous NTD-affected pregnancy or other very-high-risk situations; they may need higher doses and should discuss it with their clinician. [[ref:uspstf-2023-folic-acid]]
items.body:
NICE is specific: offer 5 mg a day of folic acid, when planning and in the first 12 weeks, when there is an increased risk of NTD or other congenital malformation. Examples it gives: NTD or malformation in the person, their partner or family; a previous affected pregnancy; type 1 or 2 diabetes; a haematological condition requiring folic acid (sickle cell disease, thalassaemia); or medicines that affect folate absorption or metabolism, such as anti-epileptics or HIV medicines. [[ref:nice-2025-ng247]]

After bariatric surgery, NICE refers to the bariatric unit for individual advice on folic acid and other micronutrients. [[ref:nice-2025-ng247]]
items.recall: Which situations, per NICE, justify high-dose folic acid?
items.application: Before “giving the usual folic acid”, review NTD history, diabetes, haemoglobinopathies, bariatric surgery and medicines (especially anti-epileptics). If any is present, the dose belongs to an individual plan with local guidance and the relevant specialist (neurology, endocrinology, haematology). Local doses: in Spain, the national guideline (2014) gives 0.4 mg/day, or 5 mg/day with a history of NTD, diabetes or anticonvulsants. In Argentina, the Ministry of Health gives 0.4 mg/day from 3 months before, or 4 mg/day after a previous baby with an NTD. [[ref:guiasalud-2014-gpc-embarazo]] [[ref:msal-ar-acido-folico]]
items.pearl: Mind the units: 400 µg is 0.4 mg; 5 mg is more than ten times that dose. Mixing up µg and mg on a prescription is a classic error.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NICE NG247 (2025); USPSTF 2023 excludes high risk.

items.title: Myth: “more folic acid, more fertility and fewer miscarriages”
items.core: In unexplained recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL), low-dose folic acid has not been shown to prevent further losses (strong recommendation); in its justification, ESHRE states that high doses should not be used without hyperhomocysteinaemia or conditions that raise NTD risk (diabetes, epilepsy). [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.body:
Strong ESHRE recommendation: low-dose folic acid has not been shown to prevent loss in unexplained RPL. In its justification, ESHRE adds that high doses should not be used without hyperhomocysteinaemia or NTD-risk conditions. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

NICE adds two common clinic situations in which there is no need to go above 400 µg a day, unless another risk factor from its list is present: BMI ≥25 kg/m² and increased risk of pre-eclampsia. [[ref:nice-2025-ng247]]
items.recall: Does folic acid prevent unexplained recurrent pregnancy loss?
items.application: If a patient with recurrent miscarriage asks for “the high dose” so as not to lose again, you can explain that the standard dose is still for NTD prevention and that there is no evidence that increasing it protects against miscarriage.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE RPL 2022: strong (low dose not shown to prevent loss); the caution on high doses is in the justification; NICE NG247.

items.title: Reading the prenatal label: what to look for and avoid
items.core: During pregnancy, cod liver oil and supplements containing vitamin A (retinol) should not be taken, and this may include regular multivitamins not designed for pregnancy. [[ref:nice-2025-ng247]]
items.body:
USPSTF accepts folic acid as a single supplement or within a multivitamin that contains it. [[ref:uspstf-2023-folic-acid]] ESHRE, when RPL patients ask about multivitamins, recommends steering them to products safe in pregnancy (good practice): they are not a treatment, but some vitamins (A, E) may cause harm. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

For iodine, the 2026 ATA guideline suggests a 150 µg/day supplement in women at risk of deficiency (conditional, moderate certainty) and recommends avoiding sustained supplement use above 500 µg/day in pregnancy (strong, moderate certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.recall: Which component should be avoided in a multivitamin during pregnancy per NICE?
items.application: Review her product with the patient: folic acid at the appropriate dose, no supplement-level retinol and, if it contains iodine, how much it provides per day. Ask her not to stack products on her own without discussing it.
items.pearl: “Prenatal” is a marketing label, not a guarantee of composition: reading the label is part of the visit.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NICE NG247; USPSTF 2023; ESHRE RPL (GPP); ATA 2026 (Recommendations Table 3).

items.stem: A healthy 29-year-old woman with no NTD history or medicines wants to try to conceive in a few months. Per USPSTF 2023, which is correct?

options.text: Folic acid 0.4–0.8 mg daily from at least 1 month before conception through the first 2–3 months of pregnancy.
options.why: Correct: this is the USPSTF grade A recommendation.

options.text: Start folic acid once pregnancy is confirmed, since before that it adds no benefit.
options.why: The neural tube closes very early; that is why it should start at least 1 month before conception.

options.text: Folic acid 5 mg daily, because more dose means more protection.
options.why: High doses are reserved for increased-risk situations; this woman has none.

options.text: No supplement is needed if her diet includes fortified foods.
options.why: USPSTF and NICE recommend the supplement even with fortification.

items.explanation: Standard dose, starting before conception and continuing into the first trimester: that is how the neural-tube closure window is protected.

items.stem: Per NICE NG247, which of these women planning pregnancy has an indication for high-dose folic acid (5 mg/day)?

options.text: 31-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes.
options.why: Correct: type 1 or 2 diabetes is among NICE’s increased-risk factors.

options.text: 34-year-old woman with BMI 31 kg/m² and no other factors.
options.why: NICE states that BMI ≥25 does not require more than 400 µg unless another risk factor is present.

options.text: 30-year-old woman at increased risk of pre-eclampsia and no other factors.
options.why: NICE explicitly reassures: pre-eclampsia risk does not require going above 400 µg.

options.text: 33-year-old woman heterozygous for MTHFR C677T.
options.why: Carrying a common MTHFR variant is not listed as an indication; carriers process folic acid.

items.explanation: High doses respond to specific factors (NTD history, diabetes, haemoglobinopathies, folate-altering medicines), not to weight or a common genotype.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with three early miscarriages, unremarkable RPL work-up, no diabetes or epilepsy. She asks for high-dose folic acid “so I don’t lose it again”. Per ESHRE, what is appropriate?

options.text: Keep the low preconception dose to prevent NTDs and explain that it has not been shown to prevent loss; do not use a high dose without an indication.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE (strong): low-dose folic acid has not been shown to prevent loss; according to its justification, high doses should not be used without an indication.

options.text: Prescribe 5 mg daily: RPL is an NTD risk factor.
options.why: Unexplained RPL is not among the factors justifying a high dose.

options.text: Stop folic acid because it has no effect on RPL.
options.why: It has not been shown to prevent loss, but it is still indicated to prevent NTDs.

options.text: Switch to high-dose methylfolate, which does prevent loss.
options.why: There is no verified evidence supporting that claim.

items.explanation: Separate the outcomes: folic acid prevents NTDs; it has not been shown to prevent recurrent pregnancy loss.

items.title: Myth: “with MTHFR you can’t use folic acid”
items.core: People with an MTHFR variant can process all types of folate, including folic acid, and folic acid is the only type of folate shown to help prevent NTDs. [[ref:cdc-mthfr-folic-acid]]
items.body:
According to CDC, common variants are not a reason to avoid folic acid, and in the US more people have one or two copies of C677T than don't. [[ref:cdc-mthfr-folic-acid]] ACOG cites C677T homozygosity of 10–16% in European populations. [[ref:acog-2018-pb197-thrombophilia]]

What remains open is how much these variants slow folate metabolism: USPSTF lists it as a research need, not as a reason to change the recommendation. [[ref:uspstf-2023-folic-acid]] That 5-methyltetrahydrofolate (methylfolate) is “better” in carriers is a hypothesis, not a demonstrated result for NTD prevention.
items.recall: Can an MTHFR C677T carrier use folic acid to prevent NTDs?
items.application: If a patient brings an MTHFR report and has stopped folic acid out of fear, the priority is that she resumes NTD prevention.
items.pearl: A variant carried by most of the US population cannot, on its own, be a “disease” that contraindicates folic acid.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: CDC (public health); ACOG PB 197; USPSTF 2023 leaves it as a research area.

items.title: What I would not order: routine MTHFR genotype or homocysteine
items.core: ACOG (PB 197, 2018) does not recommend screening with MTHFR mutation analyses or fasting homocysteine, because of the lack of association between C677T variants and adverse pregnancy outcomes, including venous thromboembolism (Level B). [[ref:acog-2018-pb197-thrombophilia]]
items.body:
ACOG adds that MTHFR mutations by themselves do not appear to increase VTE risk, either outside or during pregnancy, and that evidence is insufficient to include them in thrombophilia work-up. [[ref:acog-2018-pb197-thrombophilia]]

For folic acid, the result would not change management either: the preconception recommendation is the same with or without a common variant. [[ref:cdc-mthfr-folic-acid]]
items.recall: Why does ACOG not recommend screening MTHFR or homocysteine in pregnancy?

rows.text: Thrombophilia or pregnancy-loss work-up: not recommended (ACOG)
Choosing the folate type: does not change management (CDC)

visual.alt: Diagram: ordering MTHFR or homocysteine is not recommended to investigate thrombophilia or losses (ACOG) and does not change folate choice (CDC).

items.application: A “positive” MTHFR result can bring anxiety, expensive supplements and sometimes anticoagulation without indication. Not ordering it is also care.

items.title: Patient phrase: “my test says MTHFR”
items.core: Core message, backed by CDC: the variant is very common, your body processes folic acid and folic acid is the one shown to prevent NTDs. [[ref:cdc-mthfr-folic-acid]]
items.body:
One way to put it: “Having this variant is very common: in the United States, for example, more people have it than don’t. It doesn’t mean you can’t use folic acid: you process it well, and it’s the form shown to prevent neural tube defects in the baby.” [[ref:cdc-mthfr-folic-acid]]

If she also asks about clots or miscarriage: “On its own, this variant hasn’t been linked to more clots or worse pregnancy outcomes, so guidelines don’t use it to decide treatments.” [[ref:acog-2018-pb197-thrombophilia]]
items.recall: How would you explain to a patient that her MTHFR variant does not contraindicate folic acid?
items.application: Validate the concern before correcting the fact, and write down what to take and at what dose.

items.stem: A 30-year-old patient trying to conceive brings an “MTHFR C677T heterozygous” genotype from a commercial lab and has stopped folic acid because she read she “can’t metabolise it”. Which answer fits the sources?

options.text: Resume folic acid at the standard dose: carriers process folic acid and it is the form with proven efficacy against NTDs.
options.why: Correct: this is CDC’s position; the common variant is not a reason to avoid it.

options.text: Replace it with methylfolate, which has been shown to prevent NTDs better in carriers.
options.why: CDC states folic acid is the only folate type shown to prevent NTDs; methylfolate superiority is a hypothesis.

options.text: Order fasting homocysteine before deciding.
options.why: ACOG does not recommend fasting homocysteine screening in pregnancy, and it would not change the folic acid recommendation.

options.text: Prescribe 5 mg folic acid to compensate for the variant.
options.why: A common variant is not among NICE’s high-dose indications.

items.explanation: The common variant does not change the recommendation: standard-dose folic acid, with no extra tests.

items.stem: When reviewing a thrombophilia panel for a pregnant woman, which test does ACOG not recommend?

options.text: MTHFR genotype and fasting homocysteine.
options.why: Correct: ACOG does not recommend this screening due to the lack of association with adverse outcomes (Level B).

options.text: None: the more tests, the better the stratification.
options.why: More tests without clinical utility create false “positives”, anxiety and unindicated treatment.

options.text: MTHFR yes, because C677T homozygosity clearly increases VTE risk.
options.why: ACOG states MTHFR mutations by themselves do not appear to increase VTE risk.

items.explanation: MTHFR and homocysteine add nothing to thrombophilia evaluation in pregnancy according to ACOG.

items.title: Iodine: 250 µg total; 150 µg supplement if at risk
items.core: The 2026 ATA guideline recommends that pregnant and lactating women strive for a daily iodine intake of 250 µg, with diet complemented by supplements as required (strong, moderate certainty). For women at risk of iodine deficiency given geographic region, dietary restrictions or malabsorption, it suggests a 150 µg/day supplement, ideally from at least 3 months before planned pregnancy until lactation is complete (conditional, moderate certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.body:
Nuance: the graded table recommendation is limited to women at risk, but the accompanying text advises 150 µg/day for all women preconception, in pregnancy and in lactation (unless high iodine intake is evident from traditional dietary habits) and allows higher amounts at increased risk, for example not using iodised salt, not eating dairy or following a vegan diet. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]

Mechanism: in pregnancy thyroid hormone requirements and renal iodine excretion increase, and the fetus adds demand; the sodium/iodide symporter (NIS) mediates maternal and fetal thyroid uptake and the placental transfer of iodide. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]

There are no validated biomarkers of an individual’s chronic iodine intake: urinary iodine is interpreted only as a population median. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.recall: How much total iodine does the 2026 ATA guideline recommend in pregnancy and lactation, and for whom does it suggest a 150 µg/day supplement?
items.application: In Spain, the national guideline (2014; flagged by GuíaSalud as out of date, no update found) suggests iodised salt and no routine iodine supplement before pregnancy; in pregnancy, potassium iodide 200 µg/day only if the diet falls short (3 servings of dairy and 2 g of iodised salt a day). In Argentina, the law requires all salt for food use to be iodised. Ask about diet (iodised salt, dairy, vegan diet) before applying the ATA figure. [[ref:guiasalud-2014-gpc-embarazo]] [[ref:ar-1997-ley-24786-sal-yodada]]
items.pearl: Mind the units: iodine is dosed in micrograms (µg). A product listing iodine in “mg” deserves a second look.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ATA 2026, Recommendations Table 3: 250 µg (strong, moderate); 150 µg if at risk (conditional, moderate). The accompanying text advises it for all.

items.title: Iodine and thyroid disease: the same approach
items.core: The 2026 ATA guideline suggests applying similar iodine supplementation recommendations to pregnant women taking antithyroid drugs for Graves’ hyperthyroidism and to those taking levothyroxine for hypothyroidism (conditional, low certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.body:
This is a change: the 2017 ATA guideline considered it unnecessary to start the supplement in these patients (weak recommendation, low quality), and the 2026 guideline replaces it. [[ref:ata-2017-thyroid-pregnancy]] [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]

High-dose iodine is reserved for specific therapeutic uses: the ATA exempts saturated solution of potassium iodide (SSKI) in preparation for Graves’ disease surgery (with no safety data in pregnancy, although it considers short-term preoperative use unlikely to harm the fetus) and, based on limited data, describes potassium iodide (up to 50 mg/day) as an alternative treatment for Graves’ disease in pregnancy in iodine-sufficient populations, particularly when there is higher risk or contraindications (e.g., allergies) to the usual therapies. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.recall: What does the 2026 ATA guideline suggest about iodine in pregnant women taking levothyroxine or antithyroid drugs?
items.application: If she takes levothyroxine or antithyroid drugs, do not omit iodine for that reason: assess her intake and deficiency risk as in any other patient and keep thyroid follow-up coordinated with whoever manages it.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ATA 2026, Recommendations Table 3: conditional, low certainty. Reverses the 2017 ATA position.

items.title: Iodine excess: supplements, amiodarone and contrast
items.core: The 2026 ATA guideline recommends avoiding sustained excessive dietary iodine intake and supplement use above 500 µg/day in pregnancy, because of concerns for fetal and maternal thyroid dysfunction (strong, moderate certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.body:
It also recommends avoiding excessive iodine exposure in pregnancy, except for certain medical indications, such as SSKI or iodinated contrast (strong, moderate certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]

For medications or tests that cause high iodine exposure, such as amiodarone or iodinated contrast, the guideline asks clinicians to weigh risks and benefits; the FDA currently classifies amiodarone as posing possible human fetal risk, although the guideline recognises that its potential benefits may warrant use in pregnant women. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.recall: What sustained iodine intake threshold does the 2026 ATA guideline recommend avoiding in pregnancy, and why?
items.application: In the supplement history, ask specifically about seaweed, kelp and “thyroid support” products, and check on the label how much iodine they provide per day.
items.pearl: With iodine, risk is U-shaped: both deficiency and excess disturb the thyroid, including the fetal one.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ATA 2026, Recommendations Table 3: strong, moderate certainty.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman with hypothyroidism well controlled on levothyroxine, 6 weeks pregnant. She takes a prenatal with folic acid and no iodine. Per the 2026 ATA guideline, what is most appropriate regarding iodine?

options.text: Apply the same iodine recommendation as for other pregnant women (250 µg/day total; a 150 µg/day supplement if at risk of deficiency): levothyroxine does not exclude it.
options.why: Correct: the 2026 ATA guideline suggests applying similar recommendations to women taking levothyroxine (conditional, low certainty).

options.text: Do not start iodine: on levothyroxine it is not needed.
options.why: That was the 2017 ATA position; the 2026 guideline, which replaces it, suggests the opposite.

options.text: Add 500 µg/day of iodine to compensate for the hypothyroidism.
options.why: There is no indication for high doses, and it sits at the threshold the ATA recommends not exceeding on a sustained basis.

options.text: Measure urinary iodine to decide the dose.
options.why: The ATA notes there are no validated biomarkers of individual chronic intake; urinary iodine is interpreted as a population median.

items.explanation: The 2026 ATA guideline reverses the 2017 position: taking levothyroxine or antithyroid drugs does not exclude the iodine recommendation.

items.stem: A patient planning pregnancy takes a kelp supplement “for the thyroid” whose label states 1000 µg of iodine per daily dose. Per the 2026 ATA guideline, what would you tell her?

options.text: To stop it: sustained use of supplements providing more than 500 µg/day of iodine should be avoided in pregnancy, and there is no point continuing 1000 µg/day while trying to conceive, as pregnancy can occur at any time.
options.why: Correct: the 2026 ATA guideline recommends avoiding this exposure in pregnancy (strong, moderate certainty) because of concerns for fetal and maternal thyroid dysfunction; it is best corrected before conception.

options.text: To keep it: more iodine better protects the fetal thyroid.
options.why: Excess is also a risk: the ATA recommends avoiding excessive iodine exposure in pregnancy.

options.text: To keep it, but only until the positive pregnancy test.
options.why: The pre-pregnancy approach the ATA suggests is a 150 µg/day supplement in women at risk, ideally from at least 3 months before, not a high dose stopped at the positive test.

items.explanation: Iodine has a window: 250 µg/day total in pregnancy, a 150 µg supplement if there is a risk of deficiency, and nothing above a sustained 500 µg/day.

items.stem: Per the 2026 ATA guideline, what role does urinary iodine concentration play in deciding iodine for an individual woman planning pregnancy?

options.text: No reliable role: there are no validated biomarkers of individual chronic intake, and the decision rests on risk factors for deficiency.
options.why: Correct: the guideline stresses that urinary iodine is interpreted only as a population median and that individual risk factors should still be considered.

options.text: An individual urinary iodine below 150 µg/L confirms deficiency and mandates supplementation.
options.why: The ATA urinary iodine ranges (100–199 µg/L outside pregnancy and lactation; 150–249 µg/L in pregnant women) are population medians, not individual cut-offs.

options.text: Maternal TSH replaces urinary iodine as a marker of iodine status.
options.why: The guideline states that thyroid function tests are not sensitive indicators of population iodine status, including in pregnant and postpartum women.

options.text: It is measured to set the exact supplement dose between 50 and 300 µg/day.
options.why: 50–300 µg/day is the range of doses used in studies, in line with each population’s background intake; it is not a scale to adjust by individual urinary iodine.

items.explanation: Without a valid individual biomarker, the ATA bases its formal suggestion on risk (region, dietary restrictions, malabsorption); its text goes further and advises 150 µg/day for all as a public-health measure.

items.title: Vitamin D: empiric in pregnancy, no routine 25(OH)D
items.core: The Endocrine Society suggests empiric vitamin D during pregnancy (conditional, low certainty) and suggests against routine 25(OH)D testing in healthy pregnant individuals without an established indication (conditional, very low certainty). [[ref:endo-2024-vitamin-d]]
items.body:
Indication: possible reduction of pre-eclampsia, intrauterine mortality, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth and neonatal mortality. Trials used 600 to 5000 IU (15–125 µg) daily equivalent; the guideline acknowledges the optimal dose is unclear and asks to stay within the IOM tolerable upper intake level. [[ref:endo-2024-vitamin-d]]

Before pregnancy, in healthy adults under 50, the same guideline suggests no supplementation above the recommended intake (600 IU [15 µg] a day) and no routine 25(OH)D testing, noting that 25(OH)D thresholds with outcome benefit have not been established in trials. None of this applies to people with an established indication, such as hypocalcaemia. [[ref:endo-2024-vitamin-d]]
items.recall: What does the Endocrine Society 2024 suggest about supplementing and testing vitamin D in pregnancy?
items.application: Correcting a deficiency documented for a clinical indication is different from empiric supplementation: make clear in the record which of the two you are doing and why.
items.pearl: 1 µg of vitamin D = 40 IU: 15 µg = 600 IU. Always check which unit the label uses.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Endocrine Society 2024: conditional; low (supplement) and very low (no testing) certainty.

items.title: Discrepancy: conditional guideline versus Cochrane “very uncertain”
items.core: The 2024 Cochrane review, after removing 20 studies over trustworthiness concerns, concludes that the effect of vitamin D alone on pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes and preterm birth is very uncertain. [[ref:cochrane-2024-vitd-pregnancy]]
items.body:
In the vitamin D versus placebo or nothing comparison (8 studies, 2313 pregnant women), it may reduce severe postpartum haemorrhage (a single study, low certainty) and low birthweight, although the interval does not rule out an increase. The authors call for large, rigorous trials, including on maternal adverse effects. [[ref:cochrane-2024-vitd-pregnancy]]

The Endocrine Society suggests supplementation with low certainty. [[ref:endo-2024-vitamin-d]] This is not a head-on contradiction: a conditional recommendation with low certainty and a review finding very uncertain effects describe the same gap in high-quality evidence.
items.recall: What changed in the 2024 Cochrane review on vitamin D in pregnancy, and what does it conclude?

rows.text: Endocrine Society 2024: suggests empiric (conditional, low certainty)
Cochrane 2024: very uncertain effects on pre-eclampsia, GDM and preterm birth

visual.alt: Comparison: the Endocrine Society 2024 suggests empiric vitamin D in pregnancy with low certainty; Cochrane 2024 finds very uncertain effects on pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes and preterm birth.

items.pearl: When a review removes studies for trustworthiness, earlier “moderate” estimates can disappear. Check the version and date of the review you cite.

evidence.label: limited
evidence.note: Cochrane 2024: low to very low certainty.

items.title: Vitamin D and IVF: association is not efficacy
items.core: In assisted-reproduction cohorts, vitamin D-replete women had more live births (OR 1.33; 95% CI 1.08–1.65), but this is an observational association and the authors call for a trial to test whether correcting deficiency helps. [[ref:chu-2018-vitd-art]]
items.body:
The SUNDRO RCT tested it in 630 women with 25(OH)D <30 ng/mL, normal weight and preserved reserve: a single 600,000 IU dose of vitamin D3 before IVF did not improve clinical pregnancy (37% vs 40%; RR 0.91; 95% CI 0.75–1.11), and no exploratory subgroup benefited. [[ref:somigliana-2021-sundro]]

A 2023 meta-analysis mixing 9 RCTs and 3 cohorts reports more clinical pregnancy (OR 1.70), with high heterogeneity, six studies using multicomponent products (e.g. with inositol or melatonin) and no pooling of live births; with vitamin D alone the effect was not significant unless SUNDRO was excluded. [[ref:meng-2023-vitd-infertility]]
items.recall: What did the SUNDRO RCT show about vitamin D before IVF?

rows.text: Cohorts: replete vitamin D ↔ more live births
SUNDRO RCT: no improvement in clinical pregnancy
Mixed meta-analysis: clinical pregnancy, live birth not pooled

visual.alt: Diagram: in cohorts, replete vitamin D is associated with more live births; the SUNDRO RCT showed no improvement in clinical pregnancy with supplementation; a mixed meta-analysis reports clinical pregnancy without pooling live births.

items.application: If a woman going to IVF is supplemented, let it be for general reasons (pregnancy, deficiency with an indication), not with a promise of more pregnancies.
items.pearl: Always ask: association or trial? Clinical pregnancy or live birth? Vitamin D alone or a “cocktail”?

evidence.label: insufficient
evidence.note: Cohorts (association); one negative RCT; mixed meta-analysis of limited quality.

items.title: Recurrent pregnancy loss: vitamin D may be considered, testing it not
items.core: ESHRE proposes that preconception counselling in RPL may include considering prophylactic vitamin D (good practice), although evidence of effectiveness is absent, and does not recommend testing vitamin D to find a cause or guide treatment. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.body: The reasoning: deficiency seems common in women with RPL (47.4% below 30 ng/mL in a case-control study) and is associated with obstetric complications, but there is no indication that vitamin D status contributes to RPL, nor studies measuring its effect on live birth in the next pregnancy. The guideline considers supplementation safe. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.recall: What does ESHRE say about testing and supplementing vitamin D in RPL?
items.application: You can offer it as a general pregnancy-health measure, explaining that it is not a treatment for recurrent loss.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE RPL 2022: good practice point (GPP), no evidence of effectiveness.

items.stem: A healthy pregnant woman at 10 weeks, no hypocalcaemia or other indication. Per the Endocrine Society 2024, what is appropriate regarding vitamin D?

options.text: Consider an empiric supplement without routine 25(OH)D testing.
options.why: Correct: it suggests empiric vitamin D and against routine 25(OH)D testing (both conditional).

options.text: Measure 25(OH)D and supplement only if <30 ng/mL.
options.why: The guideline suggests against routine testing and notes no trial-established benefit thresholds.

options.text: Measure 25(OH)D every trimester to adjust the dose.
options.why: There is no recommendation for serial monitoring in healthy pregnant women.

options.text: Do not supplement, because evidence shows it has no effect.
options.why: The evidence is uncertain, not negative; the guideline suggests supplementation with low certainty.

items.explanation: Conditional suggestion: supplement without 25(OH)D screening, unless there is an established clinical indication.

items.stem: In the SUNDRO RCT (women with 25(OH)D <30 ng/mL before IVF), what result was obtained with a single high dose of vitamin D3 versus placebo?

options.text: It did not improve the clinical pregnancy rate (37% vs 40%).
options.why: Correct: RR 0.91 (95% CI 0.75–1.11), with no benefiting subgroups.

options.text: It significantly increased live births.
options.why: The primary outcome was clinical pregnancy and it did not improve; an increase in live births cannot be claimed.

options.text: It improved only in women with more severe deficiency.
options.why: Exploratory analyses by baseline 25(OH)D did not identify benefit.

options.text: It reduced miscarriages, though clinical pregnancy did not change.
options.why: Miscarriage was a secondary outcome; the trial does not show that vitamin D reduces it, and an effect on miscarriage cannot be claimed without an effect on clinical pregnancy.

items.explanation: The observational association was not confirmed in the trial: correcting vitamin D before IVF did not increase clinical pregnancy.

items.stem: Which statement best describes the evidence on vitamin D and assisted-reproduction outcomes in women?

options.text: Cohorts show an association between replete vitamin D and live birth, but the largest RCT showed no benefit of supplementation on clinical pregnancy.
options.why: Correct: it separates association (Chu 2018) from trial efficacy (SUNDRO 2021).

options.text: RCTs show that supplementation increases live birth.
options.why: The 2023 meta-analysis did not pool live births and SUNDRO did not improve clinical pregnancy.

options.text: Low vitamin D causes infertility, as cohorts demonstrate.
options.why: Cohorts show association, not causation; confounding is possible.

options.text: The 2023 meta-analysis proves the efficacy of vitamin D alone on live birth.
options.why: It mixes designs and multicomponent products; with vitamin D alone the effect was not significant unless SUNDRO was excluded, and live births were not pooled.

items.explanation: Association, clinical pregnancy and live birth are different rungs; for vitamin D in IVF the trial rung has not been cleared.

items.stem: Which option correctly summarises the routine folic acid schedules of USPSTF 2023 and NICE NG247?

options.text: USPSTF: 400 µg from 3 months before; NICE: 0.4–0.8 mg from 1 month before.
options.why: They are swapped.

options.text: Both: 5 mg from 1 month before until delivery.
options.why: 5 mg is the NICE dose for increased risk, not routine, and neither schedule runs to delivery.

options.text: USPSTF recommends 0.4–0.8 mg/day from at least 1 month before through the first 2–3 months of pregnancy; NICE recommends 400 µg/day, ideally from 3 months before and for at least the first 12 weeks.
options.why: Correct: they agree in substance with slightly different schedules.

options.text: Both: only once pregnancy is confirmed, until week 12.
options.why: Both ask to start before conception; NICE considers starting after a positive pregnancy test only as a fallback, as early as possible, if it was not started before.

items.explanation: Same goal (preventing neural tube defects), slightly different schedules: the practical point is to start before conception.

items.stem: A woman planning pregnancy in a country with folic acid-fortified flour asks whether she also needs a supplement. What do USPSTF and NICE answer?

options.text: No: fortification is enough.
options.why: Both keep the supplement even with fortification.

options.text: Only if a serum folate test is low.
options.why: The recommendation does not depend on measuring folate.

options.text: Only if she has been trying for more than 6 months.
options.why: The aim is to prevent neural tube defects, not to treat infertility.

options.text: Yes: both keep the supplement even where foods are fortified.
options.why: Correct: USPSTF explains that dietary intake is often insufficient; NICE advises it even with fortified flour.

items.explanation: Fortification does not replace the preconception supplement, whose aim is to prevent neural tube defects.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman with previous bariatric surgery planning pregnancy. According to NICE NG247, what is appropriate regarding folic acid?

options.text: 400 µg/day, the same as any other woman.
options.why: NICE does not simply apply the standard schedule: it refers to the bariatric unit.

options.text: Individual advice from the bariatric unit on folic acid and other micronutrients.
options.why: Correct: NICE NG247.

options.text: Methylfolate instead of folic acid, because she cannot absorb it.
options.why: NICE makes no such recommendation.

options.text: No supplement until serum folate is measured.
options.why: NICE does not make supplementation conditional on measuring folate.

items.explanation: Before giving “the usual folic acid”, review the history: bariatric surgery calls for an individual plan.

items.stem: A woman with a previous child with a neural tube defect planning another pregnancy. What daily folic acid dose do the 2014 Spanish guideline and the Argentine Ministry of Health give?

options.text: The Spanish guideline recommends 5 mg/day; the Argentine Ministry of Health gives 4 mg/day.
options.why: Correct: Spanish pregnancy guideline (2014) and the Argentine Ministry of Health glossary.

options.text: Both give 0.4 mg/day.
options.why: 0.4 mg is the standard dose; after a child with an NTD both increase the dose.

options.text: The Spanish guideline gives 4 mg/day; Argentina, 5 mg/day.
options.why: They are swapped.

options.text: Both give 0.8 mg/day.
options.why: It is not the dose either gives for this case.

items.explanation: The Spanish guideline recommends 5 mg/day with a history of NTD, diabetes or anticonvulsants; the Argentine Ministry of Health gives 4 mg/day after a child with an NTD and asks to be told about anti-epileptics or diabetes.

items.stem: When checking a folic acid prescription, which unit equivalence is correct?

options.text: 400 µg equals 4 mg.
options.why: 400 µg is 0.4 mg.

options.text: 5 mg equals 500 µg.
options.why: 5 mg is 5000 µg.

options.text: 400 µg equals 0.4 mg, and 5 mg is more than ten times that dose.
options.why: Correct: 1 mg = 1000 µg.

options.text: 0.4 mg and 5 mg are equivalent doses in practice.
options.why: The high dose is more than ten times the standard one and has specific indications.

items.explanation: Mixing up µg and mg on a prescription is a classic error: NICE uses 400 micrograms for the standard schedule and 5 mg for increased risk.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman planning pregnancy, BMI 32 kg/m², with no diabetes or other risk factors from the NICE list. What folic acid dose is appropriate according to NICE NG247?

options.text: 5 mg/day because of obesity.
options.why: NICE does not consider it necessary to exceed 400 µg for BMI ≥25 without another risk factor.

options.text: 400 µg/day: BMI ≥25 kg/m² alone does not require a higher dose.
options.why: Correct: NICE NG247.

options.text: 5 mg/day if she is also at risk of pre-eclampsia.
options.why: NICE also sees no need to raise the dose for increased pre-eclampsia risk.

options.text: No supplement, because her diet should be enough.
options.why: The standard 400 µg/day schedule still applies.

items.explanation: Two common situations in which NICE sees no need to exceed 400 µg/day unless another risk factor is present: BMI ≥25 kg/m² and increased pre-eclampsia risk.

items.stem: According to the justification in the 2022 ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss guideline, in the absence of which situations should high-dose folic acid not be used?

options.text: Three or more pregnancy losses.
options.why: The number of losses is not the condition ESHRE mentions.

options.text: Maternal age over 35.
options.why: ESHRE does not mention age as a condition.

options.text: Carrying a heterozygous MTHFR variant.
options.why: ESHRE does not mention MTHFR variants as a condition.

options.text: Hyperhomocysteinaemia or conditions that increase NTD risk, such as diabetes or epilepsy.
options.why: Correct: justification of the strong ESHRE recommendation.

items.explanation: In unexplained recurrent pregnancy loss, low-dose folic acid has not been shown to prevent losses; the high dose is for specific indications.

items.stem: A woman 8 weeks pregnant takes cod liver oil and a general multivitamin not designed for pregnancy. According to NICE NG247, what do you advise?

options.text: Keep both: more vitamins protect the pregnancy.
options.why: NICE advises against cod liver oil and vitamin A (retinol) supplements.

options.text: Keep the cod liver oil and stop only the folic acid.
options.why: It is the other way round: cod liver oil should be avoided and folic acid continued.

options.text: Stop cod liver oil and vitamin A (retinol) supplements, which may include multivitamins not designed for pregnancy.
options.why: Correct: NICE NG247.

options.text: Double the multivitamin to cover increased requirements.
options.why: Doubling increases exposure to components NICE asks to avoid.

items.explanation: “Prenatal” or not, what matters is the composition: folic acid at the right dose and no supplement-level retinol.

items.stem: A patient with recurrent pregnancy loss asks which multivitamin to take “so as not to miscarry”. What does ESHRE propose?

options.text: Steer her to products safe in pregnancy, explaining that they are not a treatment and that some vitamins (A, E) may cause harm.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE good practice point.

options.text: High-dose vitamin E as antioxidant treatment for recurrent loss.
options.why: ESHRE warns that some vitamins, such as E, may cause harm, and does not consider them treatment.

options.text: Any multivitamin will do.
options.why: ESHRE asks to steer towards products safe in pregnancy.

options.text: Forbid any multivitamin.
options.why: ESHRE does not forbid them: it asks to choose products safe in pregnancy.

items.explanation: Multivitamins do not treat recurrent pregnancy loss; if she takes one, it should be safe in pregnancy.

items.stem: Which fact about the frequency of the MTHFR C677T variant is correct according to the sources?

options.text: It is rare: fewer than 1% of the population carry it.
options.why: According to CDC, in the US more people carry it than not.

options.text: CDC: in the US, more people have one or two copies of C677T than none; ACOG cites 10–16% homozygosity in European populations.
options.why: Correct: CDC and ACOG PB 197.

options.text: It only exists in homozygous form, always pathological.
options.why: There are carriers of one or two copies; such a common variant is not a disease in itself.

options.text: Homozygosity affects more than 50% of European women.
options.why: ACOG cites 10–16% in European populations.

items.explanation: A variant carried by most of the US population cannot, on its own, be a “disease” that contraindicates folic acid.

items.stem: What is the status of the idea that methylfolate (5-methyltetrahydrofolate) is “better” than folic acid in MTHFR carriers?

options.text: USPSTF recommends it in carriers.
options.why: USPSTF does not change its recommendation for the variants: it leaves their effect as a research need.

options.text: CDC recommends it because carriers cannot process folic acid.
options.why: CDC says carriers process all types of folate, including folic acid.

options.text: Trials have shown it prevents more NTDs.
options.why: Folic acid is the only type of folate shown to help prevent NTDs.

options.text: It is a hypothesis: folic acid is the only type of folate shown to help prevent NTDs, and USPSTF leaves the effect of the variants as a research area.
options.why: Correct: CDC and USPSTF 2023.

items.explanation: What remains open is how much the variants slow folate metabolism; that does not change the folic acid recommendation.

items.stem: A patient with two miscarriages brings an “MTHFR C677T homozygous” result and asks whether it increases her risk of thrombosis in pregnancy. What does ACOG say?

options.text: It is a high-risk thrombophilia requiring anticoagulation.
options.why: ACOG says MTHFR mutations by themselves do not appear to increase VTE risk.

options.text: MTHFR mutations by themselves do not appear to increase VTE risk, in or outside pregnancy, and evidence is insufficient to include them in thrombophilia work-up.
options.why: Correct: ACOG PB 197.

options.text: It must be confirmed with a second genotyping.
options.why: ACOG does not recommend this test, so repeating it adds nothing.

options.text: It increases risk only in pregnancy, not outside it.
options.why: ACOG finds no increased risk either in or outside pregnancy.

items.explanation: A “positive” MTHFR result can bring anxiety, expensive supplements and sometimes anticoagulation without indication.

items.stem: A pregnant woman asks for a fasting homocysteine level “to know whether she needs an anticoagulant”. What does ACOG say?

options.text: It recommends measuring it in all pregnant women.
options.why: ACOG does not recommend screening with fasting homocysteine.

options.text: It recommends measuring it only if there were previous miscarriages.
options.why: ACOG does not recommend screening with fasting homocysteine, and does not make it conditional on previous miscarriages.

options.text: It recommends measuring it together with the MTHFR genotype to decide.
options.why: ACOG recommends neither test.

options.text: It does not recommend screening with fasting homocysteine or MTHFR analysis (Level B).
options.why: Correct: ACOG PB 197, given the lack of association of C677T variants with adverse pregnancy outcomes.

items.explanation: Not ordering a test that does not change management is also care.

items.stem: A patient trying to conceive says: “my test says MTHFR”. Which phrase matches what CDC supports?

options.text: “Your variant prevents you from using folic acid; switch to methylfolate.”
options.why: CDC says carriers process folic acid.

options.text: “It is a serious mutation; your whole family must be tested.”
options.why: It is a very common variant, not a serious mutation.

options.text: “It is a very common variant; your body processes folic acid and it is the form shown to prevent neural tube defects.”
options.why: Correct: core message backed by CDC.

options.text: “Don’t worry, you don’t need to take anything.”
options.why: Reassure, yes, but folic acid is still indicated to prevent NTDs.

items.explanation: Validate the concern before correcting the fact, and write down what to take and at what dose.

items.stem: The same patient asks whether her MTHFR variant causes clots or miscarriages. Which answer is consistent with ACOG?

options.text: “On its own, this variant hasn’t been linked to more clots or worse pregnancy outcomes, so guidelines don’t use it to decide treatments.”
options.why: Correct: ACOG PB 197.

options.text: “Yes, it explains your miscarriages.”
options.why: ACOG finds no association of C677T with adverse pregnancy outcomes.

options.text: “Only if you are homozygous, and then you need heparin.”
options.why: ACOG does not recommend MTHFR testing nor uses it to indicate treatment.

options.text: “It clearly increases the risk of thrombosis in pregnancy.”
options.why: According to ACOG, on its own it does not appear to increase VTE risk.

items.explanation: A two-part message: keep taking folic acid, and the variant on its own does not guide treatment.

items.stem: Which option summarises the graded 2026 ATA recommendations on iodine in pregnancy and lactation?

options.text: Total intake 150 µg/day; 250 µg/day supplement for everyone.
options.why: The figures are swapped.

options.text: Total intake 500 µg/day, which is the target.
options.why: 500 µg/day is the supplement threshold ATA recommends not exceeding on a sustained basis.

options.text: Strive for a total intake of 250 µg/day (strong, moderate certainty) and, in women at risk of deficiency, a 150 µg/day supplement ideally from at least 3 months before planned pregnancy until lactation ends (conditional, moderate certainty).
options.why: Correct: ATA 2026, Recommendations Table 3.

options.text: It does not recommend iodine in pregnancy.
options.why: ATA 2026 gives explicit intake and supplement recommendations.

items.explanation: Nuance: the table limits the supplement to women at risk, but the accompanying text advises 150 µg/day for all preconception, in pregnancy and in lactation, unless high intake is evident from traditional diet.

items.stem: A woman in Spain planning a pregnancy. Which option correctly describes the positions of ATA 2026 and the 2014 Spanish pregnancy guideline on iodine?

options.text: ATA suggests a 150 µg/day supplement in women at risk (and its text advises it for all); the Spanish guideline suggests iodised salt and no routine iodine supplement before pregnancy, and in pregnancy potassium iodide 200 µg/day only if the diet falls short (3 servings of dairy + 2 g of iodised salt).
options.why: Correct: ATA 2026 and the Spanish pregnancy guideline (2014).

options.text: Both recommend 200 µg/day of potassium iodide for everyone before pregnancy.
options.why: The Spanish guideline suggests no routine iodine supplementation before pregnancy.

options.text: The Spanish guideline recommends avoiding iodised salt.
options.why: On the contrary: it suggests recommending iodised salt.

options.text: ATA advises against any iodine supplement before pregnancy.
options.why: ATA suggests starting it ideally at least 3 months before planned pregnancy in women at risk.

items.explanation: ATA 2026 proposes a preconception supplement; the Spanish guideline (2014) prioritises iodised salt and dairy and reserves potassium iodide for when diet falls short. Ask about diet before applying a figure.

items.stem: In Argentina, what does Law 24,786 establish about salt?

options.text: That only table salt sold in some provinces must be iodised.
options.why: The law applies throughout the national territory.

options.text: That every pregnant woman must receive an iodine supplement.
options.why: The law regulates salt, not supplementation in pregnancy.

options.text: That iodised salt is a voluntary recommendation for industry.
options.why: It is a legal obligation, with penalties provided.

options.text: That nationwide, salt for human or animal food use must be enriched with iodine, including sodium-free or reduced-sodium salts.
options.why: Correct: Law 24,786 (1997), which replaces article 1 of Law 17,259.

items.explanation: With mandatory iodised salt, the clinical question is how much iodised salt and dairy the patient consumes, and whether she follows a vegan or salt-free diet.

items.stem: How did the ATA position on iodine in pregnant women taking levothyroxine or antithyroid drugs change between 2017 and 2026?

options.text: It did not change: both suggest not supplementing.
options.why: ATA 2026 replaces the 2017 position.

options.text: 2017 considered starting the supplement unnecessary in these patients (weak, low quality); 2026 suggests applying similar supplementation recommendations as for others (conditional, low certainty).
options.why: Correct: ATA 2017 and ATA 2026.

options.text: 2017 strongly recommended it; 2026 advises against it.
options.why: It is the other way round.

options.text: 2026 recommends high iodine doses in these patients.
options.why: It suggests recommendations similar to other pregnant women, not high doses.

items.explanation: If she takes levothyroxine or antithyroid drugs, do not omit iodine for that reason: assess her intake and risk as in any other patient.

items.stem: A woman 10 weeks pregnant with Graves’ disease on antithyroid drugs. According to ATA 2026, what is correct about iodine?

options.text: Any iodine intake is contraindicated.
options.why: ATA 2026 suggests recommendations similar to other pregnant women.

options.text: She should take potassium iodide 50 mg/day as a routine supplement.
options.why: Up to 50 mg/day is described as an alternative Graves’ treatment in specific situations, not as a routine supplement.

options.text: Supplementation recommendations similar to other pregnant women apply (conditional, low certainty); high-dose iodine is reserved for specific therapeutic uses.
options.why: Correct: ATA 2026, Recommendations Table 3.

options.text: She should stop the antithyroid drug and take iodine only.
options.why: ATA does not propose that; thyroid follow-up is coordinated with whoever manages it.

items.explanation: Distinguish nutritional intake (micrograms) from high-dose therapeutic uses: SSKI before Graves’ surgery or, based on limited data, potassium iodide (up to 50 mg/day) as an alternative for Graves’ disease in iodine-sufficient populations.

items.stem: A pregnant woman needs an imaging test with iodinated contrast. According to ATA 2026, how is it approached?

options.text: Iodinated contrast is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.
options.why: ATA lists it among the medical indications exempted from avoiding excessive exposure.

options.text: It is one of the medical indications exempted from avoiding excessive iodine exposure; risks and benefits are weighed.
options.why: Correct: ATA 2026 (strong, moderate certainty).

options.text: An extra iodine supplement should be added before the test.
options.why: Contrast already involves high iodine exposure.

options.text: It requires no special consideration.
options.why: ATA asks to weigh risks and benefits of drugs or tests with high iodine exposure.

items.explanation: With iodine, risk is U-shaped: both deficiency and excess disturb the thyroid, including the fetal one.

items.stem: A “thyroid support” supplement lists “iodine 1.5 mg” per daily dose. How do you interpret it in a woman 7 weeks pregnant, according to ATA 2026?

options.text: That is 150 µg/day: the dose suggested in women at risk.
options.why: 1.5 mg is 1500 µg, not 150 µg.

options.text: That is 15 µg/day: insufficient.
options.why: 1.5 mg is 1500 µg.

options.text: The ATA threshold refers only to diet, not supplements.
options.why: ATA recommends avoiding sustained supplement use above 500 µg/day.

options.text: That is 1500 µg/day, above the 500 µg/day that ATA recommends not exceeding on a sustained basis in pregnancy.
options.why: Correct: ATA 2026 (strong, moderate certainty), because of the risk of fetal and maternal thyroid dysfunction.

items.explanation: Iodine is dosed in micrograms: a product listing it in “mg” deserves a second look.

items.stem: A healthy 30-year-old woman planning pregnancy, with no established clinical indication, asks to measure 25(OH)D and take high-dose vitamin D. What does the Endocrine Society 2024 suggest?

options.text: Measure 25(OH)D and supplement until above 30 ng/mL.
options.why: The guideline suggests no routine testing and notes that thresholds with outcome benefit have not been established in trials.

options.text: Before pregnancy, neither supplementing above the recommended intake (600 IU/day) nor routine 25(OH)D testing.
options.why: Correct: suggestions for healthy adults under 50.

options.text: Supplement at high doses to improve fertility.
options.why: The guideline does not suggest exceeding the recommended intake before pregnancy.

options.text: Measure 25(OH)D in everyone before conceiving.
options.why: It suggests against routine testing in healthy adults without an indication.

items.explanation: Once pregnant the suggestion changes: empiric vitamin D (conditional, low certainty), still without routine 25(OH)D testing.

items.stem: The recommended vitamin D intake of 600 IU/day is equivalent to how many micrograms?

options.why: 1 µg is 40 IU: 1.5 µg would be 60 IU.

options.text: 60 µg.
options.why: 60 µg would be 2400 IU.
150 µg would be 6000 IU.

options.text: 15 µg.
options.why: Correct: 1 µg of vitamin D = 40 IU.

items.explanation: Pregnancy trials used 600 to 5000 IU (15–125 µg) daily equivalent; the optimal dose is unclear and the IOM tolerable upper intake level should be respected.

items.stem: What did the 2024 Cochrane review on vitamin D alone in pregnancy do, and what did it conclude?

options.text: It removed 20 studies over trustworthiness concerns and concludes that the effect on pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes and preterm birth is very uncertain.
options.why: Correct: Cochrane 2024.

options.text: It confirmed with high certainty that it reduces pre-eclampsia.
options.why: The effect on pre-eclampsia is very uncertain.

options.text: It showed that it increases gestational diabetes.
options.why: The effect on gestational diabetes is very uncertain, not a demonstrated increase.

options.text: It included all available studies without assessing trustworthiness.
options.why: It removed 20 studies over trustworthiness concerns.

items.explanation: When a review removes studies for trustworthiness, earlier “moderate” estimates can disappear: check the version and date of the review you cite.

items.stem: The Endocrine Society 2024 suggests empiric vitamin D in pregnancy (conditional, low certainty); Cochrane 2024 finds very uncertain effects. How are they read together?

options.text: They contradict each other: one of them is wrong.
options.why: It is not a head-on contradiction: both reflect the lack of high-quality evidence.

options.text: Cochrane shows vitamin D has no effect.
options.why: A very uncertain effect does not mean a demonstrated absence of effect.

options.text: They describe the same gap in high-quality evidence: a conditional, low-certainty suggestion and a review with very uncertain effects.
options.why: Correct: it is not a head-on contradiction.

options.text: The guideline relies on high-certainty evidence that Cochrane did not include.
options.why: The guideline itself rates its suggestion as low certainty.

items.explanation: Cochrane calls for large, rigorous trials, including on maternal adverse effects.

items.stem: A colleague cites a 2023 meta-analysis in which vitamin D increases clinical pregnancy (OR 1.70) in infertility. Which limitation is correct?

options.text: It only included low-risk-of-bias trials of vitamin D alone.
options.why: It mixed trials and cohorts, and six studies used multicomponent products.

options.text: It showed a pooled increase in live births.
options.why: It did not pool live births.

options.text: It mixed 9 RCTs and 3 cohorts, with high heterogeneity, six studies with multicomponent products and no pooling of live births; with vitamin D alone the effect was not significant unless SUNDRO was excluded.
options.why: Correct: Meng 2023.

options.text: Its result matches the SUNDRO RCT.
options.why: SUNDRO showed no improvement in clinical pregnancy.

items.explanation: Always ask: association or trial? Clinical pregnancy or live birth? Vitamin D alone or a “cocktail”?

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman with 25(OH)D of 22 ng/mL about to start IVF asks whether vitamin D “will give her better chances”. What is consistent with the evidence?

options.text: If supplemented, let it be for general reasons (pregnancy, deficiency with an indication), without promising more pregnancies: in the SUNDRO RCT clinical pregnancy did not improve.
options.why: Correct: SUNDRO was negative and the cohort association does not prove efficacy.

options.text: A single 600,000 IU dose before IVF, which improves clinical pregnancy.
options.why: That is exactly what SUNDRO tested, with no improvement (37% vs 40%).

options.text: Delay IVF until above 30 ng/mL.
options.why: No cited trial supports delaying IVF for this reason.

options.text: Cohorts prove that correcting deficiency increases live births.
options.why: Cohorts show an association; the authors call for a trial to test whether correcting deficiency helps.

items.explanation: Association is not efficacy: the RCT that tested it in deficient women showed no benefit and no exploratory subgroup benefited.

items.stem: According to the 2022 ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss guideline, what place does vitamin D have?

options.text: Measure 25(OH)D in everyone to find the cause and treat until normal.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend testing vitamin D to find a cause or guide treatment.

options.text: ESHRE advises against supplementing for lack of safety.
options.why: ESHRE considers supplementation safe and proposes it may be considered.

options.text: It is a recognised cause of recurrent loss that must be treated.
options.why: There is no indication that vitamin D status contributes to recurrent loss.

options.text: Preconception counselling may include considering prophylactic vitamin D (good practice), although there is no evidence of effectiveness, and testing it to find a cause or guide treatment is not recommended.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE 2022 good practice point.

items.explanation: You can offer it as a general pregnancy-health measure, explaining that it is not a treatment for recurrent loss.

items.stem: In a case-control study cited by ESHRE, 47.4% of women with recurrent pregnancy loss had 25(OH)D <30 ng/mL. What does ESHRE conclude?

options.text: That deficiency causes recurrent loss.
options.why: ESHRE says there is no indication that vitamin D status contributes to recurrent loss.

options.text: Deficiency seems common and is associated with obstetric complications, but there is no indication that it contributes to recurrent loss nor studies on live birth in the next pregnancy.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE 2022 reasoning.

options.text: That vitamin D must be measured in everyone to guide treatment.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend testing it for that purpose.

options.text: That supplementing increases live birth in the next pregnancy.
options.why: There are no studies measuring that effect.

items.explanation: Common and associated does not mean causal: that is why vitamin D may be considered, but is not tested to find the cause.

acog-2018-pb197-thrombophilia.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 197: Inherited Thrombophilias in Pregnancy
acog-2018-pb197-thrombophilia.authors: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists' Committee on Practice Bulletins—Obstetrics
acog-2018-pb197-thrombophilia.population: Pregnant women and women considered for inherited thrombophilia evaluation.
acog-2018-pb197-thrombophilia.finding: Because of the lack of association between heterozygosity or homozygosity for MTHFR C677T and adverse pregnancy outcomes (including VTE), screening with MTHFR mutation analyses or fasting homocysteine is not recommended (Level B). MTHFR mutations by themselves do not appear to increase VTE risk.
acog-2018-pb197-thrombophilia.limitations: Full text read (Obstet Gynecol 2018;132:e18–34) from an academic copy of the published PDF. Whether ACOG has reaffirmed or replaced it after 2018 was not verified. US context.

ar-1997-ley-24786-sal-yodada.title: Ley 24.786: sal para uso alimentario humano o animal, modificación de la Ley 17.259
ar-1997-ley-24786-sal-yodada.authors: Congreso de la Nación Argentina (texto publicado por el Ministerio de Salud, Legisalud/e-legis-ar)
ar-1997-ley-24786-sal-yodada.population: General population of Argentina (salt for food use).
ar-1997-ley-24786-sal-yodada.finding: Replaces article 1 of Law 17,259: throughout the country, salt for human or animal food use must be iodine-enriched, including sodium-free or reduced-sodium salts; selling non-iodised salt is penalised.
ar-1997-ley-24786-sal-yodada.limitations: Statute, not a clinical guideline; sets no dose for pregnancy. The original text of Law 17,259 and the ANMAT programme document could not be read (argentina.gob.ar returned HTTP 522/523).

ata-2017-thyroid-pregnancy.title: 2017 Guidelines of the American Thyroid Association for the Diagnosis and Management of Thyroid Disease During Pregnancy and the Postpartum
ata-2017-thyroid-pregnancy.authors: Alexander EK, Pearce EN, Brent GA, Brown RS, Chen H, Dosiou C, Grobman WA, Laurberg P, Lazarus JH, Mandel SJ, Peeters RP, Sullivan S
ata-2017-thyroid-pregnancy.population: Women planning pregnancy, pregnant and breastfeeding.
ata-2017-thyroid-pregnancy.finding: Total iodine intake of ~250 µg/day in pregnancy and lactation (strong, high quality); in most regions, including the US, a daily 150 µg supplement as potassium iodide, ideally from 3 months before (strong, moderate). No need to start it in pregnant women treated for hyperthyroidism or taking levothyroxine (weak, low). Avoid sustained intake >500 µg/day (strong, moderate); kelp unreliable.
ata-2017-thyroid-pregnancy.limitations: Iodine section (questions 10–11) and lactation read in the accepted, pre-copyedit manuscript; the final version in Thyroid 2017;27:315–389 may differ in wording or numbering. US-oriented; strategy depends on each country's iodine status.

ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy.title: American Thyroid Association 2026 Guidelines for Thyroid Disease in Preconception, Pregnancy, and Postpartum
ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy.authors: Korevaar TIM, Leung AM, Alexander EK, Bliddal S, Boelaert K, Brenta G, Chou R, Dhillon-Smith R, Dosiou C, Eaton JL, Guan H, Kilpatrick SJ, Lasserre BJ, Lee SY, Maraka S, Meister KD, Morris-Wiseman LF, Nguyen CT, Pearce EN, Shan Z
ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy.population: Women planning pregnancy (including those with infertility, recurrent miscarriage or fertility treatment), pregnant women and women postpartum or breastfeeding. Replaces the 2017 ATA guideline; endorsed by, among others, ESHRE, the European Thyroid Association, ACOG, the Endocrine Society and the Latin American Thyroid Society.
ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy.finding: Infertility: TSH for all women with infertility or recurrent miscarriage (GPS) and optional TPOAb (conditional, low); on levothyroxine, target TSH 0.5–2.5 mU/L (GPS). Subclinical hypothyroidism: confirm after 4–6 weeks (conditional, moderate); TSH > 10 mU/L, treat (GPS); if persistent, low-dose levothyroxine (25–75 mcg/day; 25–50 in flowchart 1) (conditional, low certainty). Euthyroid autoimmunity (TPOAb and/or TgAb): do not offer levothyroxine (strong, high), recheck TSH and FT4 every 3–6 months; no prednisolone or immunoglobulin. Pregnancy: without a laboratory-specific interval, TSH 0.1–4.0 mU/L in the first and second trimesters. Iodine: 250 mcg/day total intake in pregnancy and lactation (strong, moderate); 150 mcg/day supplement in women at risk of deficiency (conditional, moderate); avoid > 500 mcg/day. Do not offer selenium to euthyroid antibody-positive pregnant women (conditional, moderate).
ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy.limitations: Full text read in the published version deposited in the University of California repository (eScholarship). Recommendations carry no individual number: they are cited by their “Recommendations Table” and page. Strength strong (“should”) or conditional (“may”), GRADE certainty very low to high, or good practice statement (GPS). The authors acknowledge that much of the evidence is of low or moderate quality; dissenting comments from group members are in supplementary material that was not reviewed. It gives no data specific to Argentina or Spain.

cdc-mthfr-folic-acid.title: MTHFR Gene Variant and Folic Acid Facts
cdc-mthfr-folic-acid.authors: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
cdc-mthfr-folic-acid.population: People who can become pregnant, including carriers of MTHFR variants (US).
cdc-mthfr-folic-acid.finding: People with MTHFR variants can process all types of folate, including folic acid; folic acid is the only type of folate shown to help prevent neural tube defects; common variants are not a reason to avoid it. The C677T variant is very common in the US.
cdc-mthfr-folic-acid.limitations: Public-health information page (not a GRADE guideline); read in full. Date shown on the page: 16 July 2026 (not stated whether publication or review).

chu-2018-vitd-art.title: Vitamin D and assisted reproductive treatment outcome: a systematic review and meta-analysis
chu-2018-vitd-art.authors: Chu J, Gallos I, Tobias A, Tan B, Eapen A, Coomarasamy A
chu-2018-vitd-art.population: 11 cohort studies (2700 women) undergoing assisted reproduction.
chu-2018-vitd-art.finding: Vitamin D-replete women had more live births than deficient/insufficient women (OR 1.33; 95% CI 1.08–1.65; 7 studies, 2026 women); no association with miscarriage. The authors call for an RCT to test whether correcting deficiency helps.
chu-2018-vitd-art.limitations: Structured abstract read. Observational data (association, possible confounding); heterogeneous populations and protocols.

cochrane-2024-vitd-pregnancy.title: Vitamin D supplementation for women during pregnancy
cochrane-2024-vitd-pregnancy.authors: Palacios C, Kostiuk LL, Cuthbert A, Weeks J
cochrane-2024-vitd-pregnancy.population: Pregnant women in randomised trials of vitamin D alone or combined (10 studies included after trustworthiness assessment).
cochrane-2024-vitd-pregnancy.finding: After removing 20 studies over trustworthiness concerns, the effect of vitamin D alone on pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes and preterm birth is very uncertain; it may reduce severe postpartum haemorrhage (1 study) and low birthweight (an increase not ruled out).
cochrane-2024-vitd-pregnancy.limitations: Full abstract read; GRADE tables of the full text not read. Assesses pregnancy, not fertility.

endo-2024-vitamin-d.title: Vitamin D for the Prevention of Disease: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline
endo-2024-vitamin-d.authors: Demay MB, Pittas AG, Bikle DD, Diab DL, Kiely ME, Lazaretti-Castro M, Lips P, Mitchell DM, Murad MH, Powers S, Rao SD, Scragg R, Tayek JA, Valent AM, Walsh JME, McCartney CR
endo-2024-vitamin-d.population: Generally healthy population without established indications for vitamin D treatment or testing, including pregnant individuals.
endo-2024-vitamin-d.finding: Pregnancy: suggests empiric vitamin D (conditional, low certainty; trials used 600–5000 IU [15–125 µg] daily equivalent; optimal dose unclear) and suggests against routine 25(OH)D testing (conditional, very low). Adults <50: no supplementation above the recommended intake (600 IU [15 µg]) and no routine 25(OH)D testing (conditional, very low).
endo-2024-vitamin-d.limitations: Abstract, recommendation list and technical remarks read on the journal website; the full justification of the pregnancy section was not read. Does not address fertility or IVF. Does not apply to people with established indications (e.g. hypocalcaemia).

eshre-2022-rpl.title: ESHRE guideline: recurrent pregnancy loss: an update in 2022
eshre-2022-rpl.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on RPL; Bender Atik R, Christiansen OB, Elson J, et al.
eshre-2022-rpl.population: Couples with recurrent pregnancy loss (two or more losses).
eshre-2022-rpl.finding: Low-dose folic acid has not been shown to prevent loss in unexplained RPL (strong); do not use high doses without hyperhomocysteinaemia or conditions raising NTD risk (diabetes, epilepsy). Prophylactic vitamin D may be considered in preconception counselling (GPP) although evidence of effectiveness is absent; vitamin D testing to find a cause is not recommended. Multivitamins: advise options safe in pregnancy (GPP); they are not a treatment. Sperm DNA fragmentation in couples with RPL: could be considered for diagnostic purposes, using a validated test (conditional; ⊕⊕⊕○). Parental karyotyping: not routine; can be carried out after an individual risk assessment (conditional).
eshre-2022-rpl.limitations: Recommendations table and vitamin D chapter read in the full ESHRE PDF. Specific RPL population; several recommendations are good practice points (GPP), not trial-based. Recommendations on sperm DNA fragmentation and parental karyotyping checked in the HRO summary (hoad002) and in the justification of the full PDF.

guiasalud-2014-gpc-embarazo.title: Guía de práctica clínica de atención en el embarazo y puerperio
guiasalud-2014-gpc-embarazo.authors: Grupo de trabajo de la GPC de atención en el embarazo y puerperio; Ministerio de Sanidad, Servicios Sociales e Igualdad; Agencia de Evaluación de Tecnologías Sanitarias de Andalucía (AETSA); GuíaSalud
guiasalud-2014-gpc-embarazo.population: Women planning pregnancy and pregnant women in the Spanish NHS.
guiasalud-2014-gpc-embarazo.finding: Before pregnancy (good practice points): folic acid 0.4 mg/day from at least 1–2 months before; 5 mg/day with a history of NTD, a previous child with NTD, diabetes or anticonvulsants; iodised salt and no routine iodine supplement. In pregnancy: potassium iodide 200 µg/day only if the diet does not reach the recommended intake (3 servings of dairy and 2 g of iodised salt) (weak recommendation); do not routinely offer iron (weak).
guiasalud-2014-gpc-embarazo.limitations: The GuíaSalud recommendations page was read, not the full text. GuíaSalud flags documents of this guideline as out of date (over 5 years); no update was found.

meng-2023-vitd-infertility.title: Influence of Vitamin D supplementation on reproductive outcomes of infertile patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis
meng-2023-vitd-infertility.authors: Meng X, Zhang J, Wan Q, Huang J, Han T, Qu T, Yu LL
meng-2023-vitd-infertility.population: 12 studies (9 RCTs and 3 cohorts; 2352 infertile women); 6 used multicomponent products containing vitamin D.
meng-2023-vitd-infertility.finding: Higher clinical pregnancy rate with vitamin D (OR 1.70; 95% CI 1.24–2.34; I² 63%), no differences in implantation, biochemical pregnancy or miscarriage. With vitamin D alone the effect was not significant unless the SUNDRO trial was excluded. Live birth was not pooled.
meng-2023-vitd-infertility.limitations: Full text read (Europe PMC). Mixes RCTs and cohorts, high heterogeneity, co-interventions (inositol, melatonin, etc.) and highly variable regimens; no GRADE assessment.

msal-ar-acido-folico.title: Ácido fólico (glosario de salud)
msal-ar-acido-folico.authors: Ministerio de Salud de la Nación (Argentina)
msal-ar-acido-folico.finding: 0.4 mg/day from three months before conception until the first 7 weeks; after a previous baby with a neural tube defect, 4 mg/day to prevent recurrence; starting after the pregnancy is known does not prevent NTDs.
msal-ar-acido-folico.limitations: Public information page with no visible date (year is the access year). The 2023 national low-risk prenatal care guideline recommends daily iron 60 mg + folic acid 0.4 mg in pregnancy.

nice-2025-ng247.title: Maternal and child nutrition: nutrition and weight management in pregnancy, and nutrition in children up to 5 years (NG247)
nice-2025-ng247.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2025-ng247.population: People planning a pregnancy or who are pregnant, and children up to 5 years (UK).
nice-2025-ng247.finding: 400 micrograms/day of folic acid from before trying to conceive (ideally 3 months) and for at least the first 12 weeks, even with fortification; 5 mg/day for increased risk of neural tube defect (personal/family history or previous affected pregnancy, type 1 or 2 diabetes, haematological conditions requiring it, medicines affecting folate such as anti-epileptics or HIV medicines); BMI ≥25 or pre-eclampsia risk do not need more than 400 µg. Avoid supplements containing vitamin A (retinol) or cod liver oil in pregnancy.
nice-2025-ng247.limitations: Recommendations 1.1.x (folic acid and vitamins section) read on the NICE website; evidence reviews not read. UK context.

somigliana-2021-sundro.title: Single oral dose of vitamin D3 supplementation prior to in vitro fertilization and embryo transfer in normal weight women: the SUNDRO randomized controlled trial
somigliana-2021-sundro.authors: Somigliana E, Sarais V, Reschini M, Ferrari S, Makieva S, Cermisoni GC, Paffoni A, Papaleo E, Vigano P
somigliana-2021-sundro.population: 630 women aged 18–39 with 25(OH)D <30 ng/mL, BMI 18–25 and AMH >0.5 ng/mL, in their 1st–3rd IVF/ICSI cycle (Italy).
somigliana-2021-sundro.finding: A single oral dose of 600,000 IU of vitamin D3 versus placebo did not improve cumulative clinical pregnancy (37% vs 40%; RR 0.91; 95% CI 0.75–1.11); no exploratory subgroup benefited.
somigliana-2021-sundro.limitations: Structured abstract read. Primary outcome: clinical pregnancy (live birth secondary, not verified here). Single high-dose regimen; normal-weight women with preserved reserve.

uspstf-2023-folic-acid.title: Folic Acid Supplementation to Prevent Neural Tube Defects: US Preventive Services Task Force Reaffirmation Recommendation Statement
uspstf-2023-folic-acid.population: People who plan to or could become pregnant (US); does not apply to those with a previous pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect or other very-high-risk situations.
uspstf-2023-folic-acid.finding: Grade A: daily supplement containing 0.4–0.8 mg (400–800 µg) of folic acid, starting at least 1 month before conception and continuing through the first 2–3 months of pregnancy. No serious harms at usual doses; MTHFR variants are listed as a research need.
uspstf-2023-folic-acid.limitations: Statement read on the USPSTF website (full recommendation text); the JAMA evidence review was not read. US context with flour fortification; gives no dose for high risk.
